title: Wendell and the Harbor
premise: In the fog-bound harbor city of Vessing, 1899, Juniper Yarrow arrives to repair the observatory's failing master clock, the mechanism that regulates every tide bell, train schedule, and alibi in the port. While dismantling its escapement they find a sealed letter hidden in the weight chamber, naming the Yarrow family among conspirators in a customs fraud that drowned eleven dockworkers a decade ago. As the century's end approaches, Juniper must decide whether to keep their family's name buried with the clock's old secrets or force the truth on the record before the victors' historians seal the archive on New Year's Eve. They choose truth at the cost of their apprenticeship, their uncle's freedom, and nearly their own life, and the book ends with the corrected record read aloud in the harbor square as the master clock, repaired and honest, strikes midnight.
about_author: Silas Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent years cataloging port ledgers and coroner's inquests from the late nineteenth century. They write historical fiction about the people whose names survive only in margins and maintenance logs.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Hours
chapters.summary: Juniper Yarrow, apprentice clockmaker, is summoned by telegram to Vessing's observatory to repair the master clock before the century turns. Their POV establishes the workshop they're leaving, their uncle Aldous's silence about the family's harbor past, and the train journey. Emotional beat: cautious ambition shadowed by a feeling of being sent away rather than sent for.

chapters.title: Eleven Bells to Vessing
chapters.summary: Arrival in the fog-bound port city, where Juniper observes how the harbor's rhythms depend on the observatory clock. They meet Keeper Halvard Brann, the observatory's aging custodian, and his wary niece Petra. Juniper's POV. Emotional beat: wonder at the great clock tempered by the city's unspoken grief around the old dock disaster.

chapters.title: The Escapement's Complaint
chapters.summary: First inspection of the master clock; Juniper diagnoses sabotage disguised as wear. Brann dismisses it, too quickly. Juniper begins dismantling the escapement and finds tool marks no apprentice made. Emotional beat: professional pride curdling into unease as they realize someone wanted the clock failing.

chapters.title: A Letter in the Weight Chamber
chapters.summary: Deep in the weight chamber, Juniper discovers a sealed letter dated 1888, naming the Yarrow family among those who profited from falsified tide ledgers during the customs scheme that drowned eleven dockworkers. Juniper's POV, alone at night. Emotional beat: the floor dropping out of their identity; invisibility revealed as inheritance.

chapters.title: What Aldous Never Sent
chapters.summary: Juniper writes home and receives an evasive reply from Uncle Aldous. In flashback chapters interleaved, we learn the family survived the scandal by silence. Petra notices Juniper's distraction and offers an unlikely friendship. Emotional beat: loyalty to kin beginning its long war with loyalty to truth.

chapters.title: The Historian's Apprentice
chapters.summary: Juniper meets Oskar Vell, a young historian preparing the city's official centennial record, who mentions the dock inquest file is 'closed and sealed by order.' Juniper says nothing about the letter but memorizes the archive's layout. Emotional beat: the first cold calculation—truth needs a door, and doors have keepers.

chapters.title: Tide Ledgers and False Midnights
chapters.summary: Juniper cross-references clock logs with harbor tide records and finds the master clock was deliberately set four minutes fast during the winter of 1888, creating false alibis. Someone in the present is watching the observatory. Petra's POV for the first time, revealing she suspects Brann is hiding something too. Emotional beat: two investigations converging in the dark.

chapters.title: The Man Who Oils the Gears
chapters.summary: A stranger claiming to be a clock inspector arrives; Juniper recognizes him from a photograph in the letter as Corvin Ashe, one of the named conspirators, now respectable. He offers Juniper money to declare the clock beyond repair and leave. Juniper's POV. Emotional beat: temptation priced in survival—take the coin, keep the name, stay invisible.

chapters.title: Petra's Harbor
chapters.summary: Petra takes Juniper to the dockworkers' memorial and introduces them to Maren Kolve, widow of one of the drowned men, who has spent eleven years asking questions no official will answer. Petra's POV. Emotional beat: grief given faces and names; Juniper's abstract truth becomes a debt owed to the living.

chapters.title: The Inquest That Wasn't
chapters.summary: Maren shares her copy of the suppressed inquest testimony, which contradicts the official record. Juniper realizes the sealed letter was hidden in the clock by someone with a conscience—likely the old clockmaker who died before speaking. Emotional beat: the dead reaching through mechanisms; Juniper accepts they are now the letter's courier.

chapters.title: Aldous Arrives
chapters.summary: Uncle Aldous appears in Vessing unannounced, desperate, begging Juniper to burn the letter. He confesses his own small part: he carried the falsified ledgers as a boy, believing he was helping the family survive. Aldous's POV. Emotional beat: love and betrayal in the same embrace; the price of survival made flesh.

chapters.title: Four Minutes Fast
chapters.summary: Ashe escalates: Brann is dismissed on manufactured grounds, and Juniper is locked out of the observatory. Petra smuggles Juniper in through the tide tunnels. Rising tension as they work on the clock by lamplight, racing Ashe's petition to have it demolished as 'unstable.' Emotional beat: defiance kindling—the clock becomes a symbol neither side can abandon.

chapters.title: The Archive at Winter's Edge
chapters.summary: Juniper and Oskar break into the sealed records annex the night before the centennial committee locks it for the new century. They find the original inquest file and proof of the clock tampering. Oskar's POV. Emotional beat: the historian's crisis—career or conscience—and his choice to help.

chapters.title: What the Victors Will Write
chapters.summary: The centennial committee, chaired by Ashe's ally Magistrate Ellery Dunn, announces the official history will 'draw a veil over regrettable incidents.' Juniper understands the deadline: truth must be public before midnight, December 31, or be archived into oblivion. Juniper's POV. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Aldous's Bargain
chapters.summary: Aldous, terrified of ruin, strikes a deal with Ashe to testify that Juniper forged the letter. Juniper learns of it from Maren. Betrayal lands. Emotional beat: the book's darkest hour of loyalty—family choosing survival over truth, exactly as the family always has.

chapters.title: The Testimony of Gears
chapters.summary: Juniper realizes the master clock itself is evidence: its tampered escapement, hidden marks, and the old clockmaker's concealed ledger of adjustments. They plan to present the mechanism publicly at the New Year's striking, when the whole city gathers. Petra's POV. Emotional beat: hope engineered from broken parts.

chapters.title: Locked in the Tower
chapters.summary: Ashe and Dunn have Juniper trapped in the observatory on December 30, the letter confiscated, the clock's evidence chamber sealed. Brann, redeemed, helps them escape through the clock's internal ladderwork. Juniper's POV. Emotional beat: terror and trust entwined; the keeper finally choosing the truth he long guarded in silence.

chapters.title: The Longest Minute
chapters.summary: New Year's Eve. Juniper, Petra, Oskar, and Maren reach the harbor square where the centennial ceremony unfolds. Dunn reads the sanitized history. Aldous, watching, breaks: he steps forward and confesses before Ashe can silence him. Emotional beat: the climax's hinge—loyalty finally bending toward truth, at maximum cost.

chapters.title: Midnight on the Record
chapters.summary: Juniper presents the escapement and the old clockmaker's ledger to the crowd; Oskar reads the suppressed testimony aloud as the clock strikes. The city hears the eleven names. Ashe flees; Dunn's authority collapses as witnesses step forward. Emotional beat: catharsis—truth spoken into public air, irreversible, on the record before the century turns.

chapters.title: After the Striking
chapters.summary: Aftermath: the inquest reopened, the eleven dockworkers' names added to the memorial, Maren given the official apology she waited eleven years for. Aldous faces charges with dignity; Juniper visits him. Emotional beat: grief without bitterness—the price paid, counted honestly.

chapters.title: The Apprentice's Certificate
chapters.summary: Juniper, blacklisted by the guild for the scandal, is instead offered Brann's position as the observatory's keeper-in-training. They repair the final sabotage and set the clock to true time for the first time in a decade. Juniper's POV. Emotional beat: quiet restoration—measuring the world in what can be carried, and choosing to carry the truth.

chapters.title: Wendell and the Harbor
chapters.summary: Epilogue, spring 1900. Juniper keeps the clock, teaches Petra its workings, and adds a small brass plate inside the weight chamber bearing the eleven names and the old clockmaker's. The harbor keeps honest time. Final emotional beat: memory institutionalized—not a monument to victors, but a mechanism that cannot forget.
